note: Benchmarks and baseline facts for the impact story and the right-sizing feature. Every entry has a source_url and source_type (primary, secondary, company_reported).

eu_empty_space.article: Article 24 (Obligation related to excessive packaging), paragraphs 1, 3 and 5, Regulation (EU) 2025/40
eu_empty_space.definition: Art. 24(3): '(a) empty space shall mean the difference between the total volume of grouped packaging, transport packaging or e-commerce packaging and the volume of sales packaging contained therein; (b) empty space ratio shall mean the ratio of the empty space as defined in point (a) and the total volume of the grouped packaging, transport packaging or e-commerce packaging.' So ratio = (outer volume - volume of sales packaging inside) / outer volume. Art. 24(1): '...economic operators who fill grouped packaging, transport packaging or e-commerce packaging shall ensure that the maximum empty space ratio, expressed as a percentage, is 50 %.'
eu_empty_space.what_counts_as_empty: Art. 24(3): 'Space filled by filling materials, such as paper cuttings, air cushions, bubble wraps, sponge fillers, foam fillers, wood wool, polystyrene or Styrofoam chips, shall be considered as empty space.' Filler does not reduce the ratio; only a smaller outer box does. Note the denominator volume is the sales packaging (the product's own retail pack), not the bare product.
eu_empty_space.applies_to: Economic operators who fill grouped packaging, transport packaging or e-commerce packaging (Art. 24(1)). Art. 3(8): 'e-commerce packaging' means transport packaging used to deliver products in the context of sale online or through other means of distance sales to the end user. Exempt (Art. 24(5)): operators using sales packaging as e-commerce packaging, or using reusable packaging within a system for re-use; such sales packaging must still meet Article 10 (packaging minimisation).
eu_empty_space.application_date_rule: Art. 24(1): 'By 1 January 2030 or 3 years from the entry into force of the implementing acts adopted pursuant to paragraph 2, whichever is the latest'. Art. 24(2): Commission implementing acts on the calculation methodology (incl. irregular shapes, liquids, fragile goods) due by 12 February 2028. So 1 January 2030 is the earliest date; it moves later if the implementing acts are late. The Regulation as a whole applies from 12 August 2026 (Art. 71). Entry into force: twentieth day after OJ publication (OJ of 22.1.2025, so 11 February 2025 by our calculation; the text also uses 11 February 2025 as a reference date).
eu_empty_space.notes: Statute text. EUR-Lex would not render its text through WebFetch (metadata only), so the articles were read from a full copy of the Official Journal PDF (OJ L series 2025/40, 22.1.2025, OJ headers and ELI links) hosted by the Sri Lanka Export Development Board. Cite EUR-Lex as the official source. Recital 84 confirms the 50% cap, that it 'should not apply to reusable packaging', and that the Commission sets the calculation method. Art. 24(4): sales packaging must reduce empty space to the minimum necessary by 12 February 2028. Art. 24(6): review by 12 February 2032. Article 3 does not define 'empty space' or 'empty space ratio'; they are defined only in Art. 24(3). Related reuse rules: Art. 29(1) from 1 January 2030 operators using transport packaging incl. for e-commerce must ensure at least 40% is reusable within a re-use system (endeavour 70% by 2040), but Art. 29(4)(d) excludes 'cardboard boxes'; Art. 11(2) Commission to set a minimum number of rotations for reusable packaging by 12 February 2027.

reuse.system: hey circle reusable plastic shipping box vs single-use cardboard box (e-commerce)
reuse.break_even_range: 10 to 12 cycles depending on allocation method (carbon footprint)
reuse.unit_notes: Break-even in use cycles, climate impact only. Same paper: hey circle reusable bag breaks even vs cardboard box after 1 cycle, vs single-use plastic bag after 3, vs paper bag after 8 to 9; the box vs paper bag never breaks even in the range studied, and vs plastic bag only at 49 cycles under one allocation method. Raising the box from 15 to 30 cycles cuts its footprint 34 to 45%.
reuse.publisher: Sustainability (MDPI), vol. 16(11), 4723; authors Till Zimmermann and Fynn Hauschke
reuse.notes: Peer-reviewed. Return/loss rates not reported; empty return modelled as a transport leg. Key quote: 'The number of cycles achieved by reusable packaging is crucial for its environmental performance.'

reuse.system: Reusable e-commerce packaging vs single-use (Nordic LCA)
reuse.unit_notes: Baseline 'of 4 uses (75% reuse rate)'; sensitivity runs at '10 uses (90% reuse rate)'. Reuse rate here = share of packages that come back for another use, so uses = 1 / (1 - reuse rate).
reuse.publisher: Nordic Council of Ministers, TemaNord 2024:515 'LCA on reuse of packaging in the Nordics' (publisher inferred from pub.norden.org; not printed in the fetched section)
reuse.notes: Results: 'The reusable system presents lower environmental impacts in 8 out of 13 categories', but 'single-use plastic (SUPL) packaging consistently outperforms its reusable counterpart'. The reuse rate 'has to be higher than the respective break-even points to show clear benefits'. No numeric e-commerce break-even shown in this section. Delivery-leg variations 'do not influence the results remarkably'.

reuse.system: RePack reusable mailer vs single-use LDPE mailer and cardboard
reuse.unit_notes: Base case 30 cycles (chosen because savings vs a plastic mailer 'plateau after 30 cycles') and a 5% non-return rate, which RePack itself calls 'an ambitious and aspirational target'. Per-cycle footprint 57% smaller than a virgin LDPE mailer (39% vs recycled LDPE) in centralised reuse; 82% smaller (72% vs recycled LDPE) in decentralised reuse; 64% to 88% lower than 89%-recycled cardboard; still over 60% lower than cardboard at a 40% non-return rate.
reuse.publisher: RePack (citing a Fashion For Good fast-track LCA using a TU Delft method, with Otto and Zalando)
reuse.notes: Company page, no date. 95% return is an assumption, not an observed rate. Break-even uses not stated.

reuse.system: Boox reusable plastic shipping box vs single-use corrugated box
reuse.unit_notes: 'A Boox breaks even on the first use, whether the customer returns it or not.' Model assumes 12 uses and an 85% return rate ('primary data from Boox'). Boox 255.1 g vs cardboard box 453.6 g (50% recycled content).
reuse.publisher: Boox, methodology by Third Partners LLC using EcoChain LCA work
reuse.notes: Disclosure dated Dec 4, 2020. Break-even on first use is driven by comparing against a cardboard box heavier than the Boox; not independently reviewed. Loss rate not stated (15% implied by the 85% return rate).

reuse.system: Reusable e-commerce packaging pilot (WWF-Singapore with UOB, DHL Consulting, SingPost, Better Packaging Co.)
reuse.unit_notes: Observed: 'only about one in two returned the packaging' over 15,000 customer transactions (one in three customers chose reusable). WWF says 75 to 83% return is needed for compelling economics (equal to reuse 'at least four to six times'). Item can be used 'at least 10 to 20 times'. Cost S$3 per reusable item; cost per use 'averaging below S$2'.
reuse.notes: Pilot ran April to September 2022; article published April 12, 2023. Only observed real-world return rate found in this search. No emissions results from the pilot.

reuse.system: EU PPWR treatment of reusable e-commerce packaging
reuse.unit_notes: Art. 24(5): reusable packaging within a re-use system is exempt from the 50% empty space cap. Art. 29(1): from 2030 at least 40% of transport packaging incl. e-commerce must be reusable within a re-use system, but Art. 29(4)(d) excludes cardboard boxes. Art. 11(2): minimum rotations for reusable packaging to be set by delegated act by 12 Feb 2027. Art. 26(1): re-use systems must include an incentive to ensure collection.
reuse.notes: EPR fee modulation for reuse was not found in the Art. 45 text fetched. US state EPR treatment of reuse was not researched (not_found).

void_fill_density.original_value_and_unit: 10 lb per carton, 'Expanded Volume: 3.5 cubic feet' (Uline S-25477 Monster Crinkle Paper, kraft)
void_fill_density.notes: Vendor product spec. Conversion: 10 lb x 453.592 g/lb = 4,535.9 g / 3.5 cu ft = 1,296 g per cu ft (45.8 g per liter). 'Monster' is a jumbo crinkle cut, not the S-6118 standard crinkle in our library. Uline's S-6118 page lists only a 2.3 cu ft carton volume, no expanded volume.

void_fill_density.original_value_and_unit: '11 lbs per unit' (1 case), fills '13,068 cubic inches' of shipping box space (EcoEnclose 100% Recycled Ornament Paper Shred, 80# kraft, 15 in x 360 ft, accordion-folded)
void_fill_density.notes: Vendor. Volume also confirmed at https://help.ecoenclose.com/en-US/how-much-volume-does-the-case-of-ornament-paper-shred-fill-185615 ('conservative estimate'). Conversion: 13,068 / 1,728 = 7.5625 cu ft; 11 x 453.592 = 4,989.5 g / 7.5625 = 660 g per cu ft (23.3 g per liter). The 11 lb may include the case, and the volume is called conservative, so true density may be lower.

void_fill_density.original_value_and_unit: Library value from Uline S-22467 (7.58 lb per roll, 58 cu ft per roll), unchanged
void_fill_density.notes: Not re-fetched in this session; carried from the library. No independent g/cu ft figure found (Sealed Air AirPouch brochure, Oct 2019, gives film gauges 1.54 and 2 mil but no yield or weight per volume).

void_fill_density.original_value_and_unit: Library value from Uline S-258 (4.14 lb per 20 cu ft bag), unchanged
void_fill_density.notes: Not re-fetched; no independent density figure found in this session.

void_fill_density.original_value_and_unit: Relative only: per 1 m3 of fill, 'The weight of cushions filled with air is about 1/5th of the weight of paper pads.'
void_fill_density.publisher: Pregis (sells both air cushion and paper systems)
void_fill_density.notes: Vendor blog, Apr 27, 2023; unsourced ratio, no absolute weights. Derived (our arithmetic, illustration only): if air pillows are 59.3 g/cu ft, machine-made paper pads would be about 5 x 59.3 = 297 g/cu ft. Applies to dense paper pads, not loosely crumpled sheets.

No published paper-per-cubic-foot yield found. Ranpak FillPak spec sheet (2011, https://store.colonypackaging.com/uploads/downloads/FillPak.pdf) gives 30 lb paper, 30 in x 1,660 ft fanfold, 43 lb box, output up to 55 in of paper per second, but no fill volume. Ranpak AutoFill spec (https://www.shorr.com/wp-content/uploads/RANPAK-Autofill-Spec-Sheet-2025.pdf) gives only 'up to 8 boxes / minute'. Sealed Air on-demand paper page and Kite Packaging guide (expansion ratios x44 to x52 for paper systems, not convertible) gave no density.

void_fill_recommended.reason: Crinkle: keep the existing 907 g/cu ft. Two independent vendor-stated coverage figures bracket it (EcoEnclose 660, Uline Monster Crinkle 1,296), so the estimate is plausible and the roughly 15x gap with crumpled kraft is mostly real: shredded/crinkle paper is a dense decorative fill, not an efficient void fill. Show it as a range in the app. Crumpled kraft: no published yield found; keep 60 g/cu ft flagged as an estimate, but the Pregis ratio (paper pads about 5x the weight of air cushions per volume) suggests machine-made paper pads could be near 300 g/cu ft, so 60 is likely a low bound. Best fix is a 5-minute bench test: crumple paper into a 1 cu ft box until filled and weigh it.

projection.description: Linear scale-up of one real seller's own packaging swap. Packwise computes the plastic mass per order before and after the swap from its packaging library, multiplies by the seller's actual annual order count, and multiplies by 1,000 to represent 1,000 sellers with the same order volume and packaging mix. Headline output is pounds of plastic packaging avoided per year. Show alongside it (a) the non-plastic material added by the replacement so the trade-off is visible, and (b) what share of 2025 US parcel volume those orders represent, as a scale anchor. Optional context line: how much of the avoided plastic would likely not have been recycled at EPA's 2018 film recycling rate.
projection.formula: plastic_avoided_lb = 1000 * O * SUM_k[ s_k * (p_before_k - p_after_k) ] / 453.592 ; material_added_lb = 1000 * O * SUM_k[ s_k * (n_after_k - n_before_k) ] / 453.592 ; parcel_share = (1000 * O) / 23.1e9 ; optional_not_recycled_context_lb = plastic_avoided_lb * (1 - 0.10). Where O = seller's shipped orders per year; k = packaging configurations the seller uses (e.g., poly mailer + air pillow); s_k = share of orders shipped in configuration k (sums to 1); p_before_k, p_after_k = plastic grams per order from the Packwise library for current and swapped packaging; n_before_k, n_after_k = non-plastic grams per order (e.g., paper). 453.592 g per lb.
inputs_from_seller: O: shipped orders per year (from the seller's order history or their own estimate; use trailing 12 months, not peak season annualized)
s_k: share of orders by packaging configuration
Current packaging items per order (mailer type and size, void fill, tape) mapped to Packwise library weights
Chosen replacement packaging items mapped to Packwise library weights
caveats: Illustrative only: it does NOT predict that 1,000 sellers will switch; it is one seller's own numbers times 1,000.
'Similar sellers' means the same order volume and packaging mix; it does NOT claim to represent the average small US seller or to extrapolate to all sellers.

It does NOT claim ocean or environmental leakage avoided. Leakage figures (OECD, Pew, Oceana) are global, conflict with each other, and OECD reports OECD countries account for only 14% of leakage, so they cannot be applied to US sellers.
It does NOT claim a net environmental, carbon or lifecycle benefit. Paper or other replacements may weigh more and carry their own impacts; material_added_lb is shown so the trade-off is visible.
Library weights are typical values, not weighed for each seller's items. The Red Stag range is unsourced vendor data and is only a sanity check for library values, not an input to the headline.

Conservative settings: count only plastic components fully removed or replaced; if a library item has a weight range, use the low end for removed plastic and the high end for added material; no growth, no adoption curve; round down.
parcel_share uses all 2025 US parcels (Pitney Bowes), including non-e-commerce shipments, so it is a scale anchor, not a market-share claim.
The optional not-recycled line uses EPA's 2018 rate for all plastic bags, sacks and wraps, not poly mailers specifically; label it with the year and keep it out of the headline.

writeup_problem_statement: US carriers handled 23.1 billion parcels in 2025 (Pitney Bowes), and US online retail sales reached $340.2 billion in the second quarter of 2026 alone, 17.1% of all retail sales (US Census Bureau). The EPA counted 82.2 million tons of containers and packaging in US municipal waste in 2018, including 4.2 million tons of plastic bags, sacks and wraps, of which only 10% was recycled, compared with 96.5% of corrugated boxes. Small sellers make these packaging choices one order at a time: Etsy alone had 5.6 million active sellers worldwide in 2025, 89% of sellers in its 2024 Seller Census were businesses of one, and the US had 44,322 electronic shopping and mail-order employer firms in 2022 (US Census Bureau).
recycling_method_note: Recommend The Recycling Partnership's national RESIDENTIAL recycling rate by material (State of Recycling 2024, Figure 14): the share of each material generated by U.S. households that is actually recycled, after access, acceptance, participation, household capture and MRF sorting losses. It is the only source found that measures 'what happens to this material when it arrives at a U.S. home' and covers both fiber and film with one method; EPA 2018 and AF&PA figures are all-sector (commercial and industrial included) and AF&PA's covers fiber only. Materials TRP does not report (paperboard, kraft paper, molded pulp, EPS, PP film, laminates, paper-plastic mailers) are mapped to the nearest TRP category or set to 0 where the item has no residential recycling route, and each mapping is flagged is_estimate: true.
carbon_method_note: Recommended family: EPA WARM v16 (Dec 2023) cradle-to-gate RMAM at WARM's 'current mix' recycled content for paper, glass and metals, paired with EPA GHG Emission Factors Hub 2025 Table 9 end-of-life factors (also WARM v16-based, no avoided-emission credits, landfill methane included, carbon storage excluded), so production and disposal can be added without double counting. Because WARM models plastics as resin only, plastic films use the UK DESNZ 'average plastic film' primary-production factor (includes product forming; 2023 dataset read via Climatiq), and PP film and laminate add the implied forming increment (0.576 kg/kg) to WARM resin values. EPS remains resin-only (ACC GPPS 2022) and is a lower bound.
